<reason>A wins a high-quality, competitive debate. Both sides were epistemically disciplined (no fake citations) and rhetorically excellent. The decisive ground is empirical: B's two concrete findings — the Canadian census graduation gap and European dissolution differentials — were both neutralized by A's pre-committed design criterion (measure the family form, not post-separation disruption) and the input-versus-outcome distinction, and B never re-engaged that criterion after A4, instead repeating the "one frame" charge that fits convenience samples but not the multi-country registry and administrative-report evidence A cited. A's burden attack also stood: by B's own admission only the intact mother-father household has ever cleared the demanded standard, while the state already licenses stepfamilies, adopters, and single fathers without it — a point B answered for the "declaration" reading but never for the policy of placement. B landed strong structural counters (triage vs. universal declaration, "the motion's own comparator," the height analogy) that kept this close, and A's two clipped turns were real execution costs. But A answered both pressure questions directly with the required A1/A2 structure, narrowed the clash effectively, and offered the cleaner route to the motion as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A4.1–A4.2: pressed by B's Q1 to state a neutral criterion or withdraw a citation, A gave one — "administrative is not a design; exposure measurement is" — applying it both ways and challenging B to produce a from-infancy restricted version of the census finding. B's reply never defended the census identification, leaving B's case resting on mechanism and burden alone.</best_rebuttal>
